newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French capital markets received a shock on Monday when the new Socialist government honoured a campaign pledge and called for further time to consider the stability pact, due to be ratified on June 16 and 17.

While few questioned France's commitment to starting European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on time, the main concern among analysts was that the French position could cause a rift with Germany and throw the whole project into doubt.
Traders said non-residents were good sellers of bonds on Monday although local traders and short covering late in the session put the futures contract back in positive territory.

"It was an up and down, rangebound sort of day. The locals were reasonably good buyers around the lows although investors have been selling the September (bond futures) contract," a futures trader at a French bank said.

"There was a little bit of short covering on intra-day trades, but I'm surprised (the contract recovered). I don't think these comments have been taken on board. Now we're waiting for the Franco-German summit on Friday," he said.
"There's so much oppositon in Germany (to EMU) it's difficult (for them) to give anything away. I don't think the market reacted in any way to what was bad news," he said.
The 10-year bond spread snapped to minus four basis points from minus nine on Friday but it was back at minus seven.
"I don't think people are so much buying Germany. (German bonds) are outperforming as they're not being sold as much as France," Sonja Gibbs, bond analyst at Nomura International said.
The franc also fell on the news France wanted to discuss the pact in parliament on June 19, after the pact was due to be ratified at an Amsterdam summit on June 16 and 17.
It touched a low of 3.3825 per mark, down from 3.3740 late on Friday, but remained above the 3.3860 low hit after the Socialists swept to power in a June 1 election upset.

"France clearly wants EMU with the stability pact delayed or renegotiated but the question is whether the Germans will use this as a pretext to seek a delay in monetary union," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance, said.

The short end of the curve suffered along with the franc while the relatively sanguine reception of the news at the long end led to a flattening of the French yield curve. The gap between two- and 10-year bond yields narrowed five basis points.
September PIBOR tumbled to a low of 96.36 from an early high of 96.49 but had partly recovered along with the franc to settle down five basis points at 96.41.

Technical analyst said 96.40 represented a good support for the September PIBOR contract while the bond future had a very solid prop in the zone between 129.30/38. The contract hit 129.30 on Monday but quickly rebounded.
Some traders said there had been talk of investors selling French bonds to buy U.S. bonds and avoid a period of volatility as the doubts about monetary union continued.
Others were simply relieved to see the volatility in the Paris market place attracting interest from non-resident investors. "I don't care which way it goes as long as it moves," one broker said.
